procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 05.10.2006 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in CRLR No.366 of 2006.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Delhi High Court answered the question by holding that the respondent accused was entitled to the benefit of the said provision. Accordingly, the High Court took the view that the matter required fresh consideration for grant of previous approval under Section 6A(1) of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Aggrieved, the C.B.I. is in appeal before us.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the declaration of a statute as invalid by a court applies prospectively or retrospectively, and if an accused can claim the benefit of a law that was in force at the time of the alleged offense but was later declared unconstitutional.
appellant_arguments: If a court, while declaring a statute to be invalid, does not expressly state that the declaration has retrospective application, it should be deemed to apply only prospectively.
respondent_arguments: The respondent should get the benefit of any protection available under the law that existed at the time the offense was allegedly committed, in line with Articles 20 and 21 of the Constitution.
A similar protective provision, Section 17(A) of the PC Act, 1988, is currently in existence, which supports the respondent's interest.

cases.principle: A provision that is only a rule of evidence and does not create a new offence is not retrospectively hit by Article 20(1) of the Constitution.

Article 20(1) of the Constitution prohibits conviction or sentence under an ex post facto law, but does not prohibit a trial from being conducted under a procedure different from what existed at the time of the commission of the offence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A law declared unconstitutional is considered void from its inception (ab initio) and is treated as non-existent (non est) for all purposes.
obiter: A statute made by a competent legislature is presumed to be constitutional and remains valid until it is declared unconstitutional by a court of law.
The argument that if a court, while declaring a statute invalid, does not expressly state it applies retrospectively, it should be deemed to apply prospectively.
The submission that where a law has been in force for a long time and is subsequently repealed, it would not affect rights that had accrued during its existence.
The argument that a law declared unconstitutional only becomes inoperative or ineffective from the time of the declaration, not before.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court did not decide the substantive issue of whether a declaration of unconstitutionality applies retrospectively or prospectively. Instead, having regard to the constitutional importance of the question, the court referred the matter to a larger bench for an authoritative decision.
legal_tests_applied: The settled proposition that a declaration of unconstitutionality renders a law to be non est, void ab initio, or unenforceable.
A law made in derogation or in excess of legislative power is ab initio void.

The court distinguished between the 'repeal' of a statute and a 'declaration of unconstitutionality', finding that Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which deals with the effect of a repeal, has no application in a case where a statutory provision is declared invalid and unconstitutional.
why_appellant_lost: The court did not rule on the merits of the appeal; it referred the central question to a larger bench for a final decision.
why_respondent_won: The court did not rule on the merits of the appeal; it referred the central question to a larger bench for a final decision.
policy_considerations: The referral of the question to a larger bench under Article 145(3) of the Constitution was made to ensure that an authoritative pronouncement is made on a substantial question of constitutional law.
